claim: OVO is required for female germline viability in Drosophila.
source: OVO is required for female germline viability and has been shown to positively regulate its own expression, as well as a downstream target, ovarian tumor, by binding to the transcriptional start site (TSS).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and is a well-established finding in the field.

claim: OVO positively regulates its own expression by binding to the transcriptional start site.
source: OVO is required for female germline viability and has been shown to positively regulate its own expression, as well as a downstream target, ovarian tumor, by binding to the transcriptional start site (TSS).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Lü et al., 1998; Bielinska et al., 2005; Lü and Oliver, 2001).

claim: OVO positively regulates ovarian tumor (otu) by binding to the transcriptional start site.
source: OVO is required for female germline viability and has been shown to positively regulate its own expression, as well as a downstream target, ovarian tumor, by binding to the transcriptional start site (TSS).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: OVO preferentially binds in close proximity to target TSSs genome-wide.
source: OVO preferentially binds in close proximity to target TSSs genome-wide, is associated with open chromatin, transcriptionally active histone marks, and OVO-dependent expression.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data presented in the manuscript showing enrichment of OVO binding near TSSs.

claim: OVO binding is associated with open chromatin.
source: OVO preferentially binds in close proximity to target TSSs genome-wide, is associated with open chromatin, transcriptionally active histone marks, and OVO-dependent expression.
evidence: This is supported by integration of ChIP-seq data with ATAC-seq data showing overlap.

claim: OVO binding is associated with transcriptionally active histone marks.
source: OVO preferentially binds in close proximity to target TSSs genome-wide, is associated with open chromatin, transcriptionally active histone marks, and OVO-dependent expression.
evidence: This is supported by integration of ChIP-seq data with histone ChIP-seq data (H3K27ac, H3K4me3).

claim: OVO binding is associated with OVO-dependent gene expression.
source: OVO preferentially binds in close proximity to target TSSs genome-wide, is associated with open chromatin, transcriptionally active histone marks, and OVO-dependent expression.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq comparing hypomorphic and rescue OVO alleles.

claim: The OVO DNA binding motif is 5'-TAACNGT-3'.
source: Motif enrichment analysis on OVO ChIP peaks identified a 5'-TAACNGT-3' OVO DNA binding motif spatially enriched near TSSs.
evidence: This is derived from de novo motif analysis on ChIP-seq peaks and comparison with previously identified motifs.

claim: The OVO DNA binding motif does not exhibit precise motif spacing relative to the TSS characteristic of RNA polymerase II complex binding core promoter elements.
source: However, the OVO DNA binding motif does not exhibit precise motif spacing relative to the TSS characteristic of RNA polymerase II complex binding core promoter elements.
evidence: This is based on analysis of motif distribution relative to TSSs in CAGE-seq data.

claim: 525 genes that are bound by OVO and increase in expression downstream of OVO are known to be essential maternally expressed genes.
source: Integrated genomics analysis showed that 525 genes that are bound and increase in expression downstream of OVO are known to be essential maternally expressed genes.
evidence: This is based on integration of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data with GO term analysis.

claim: OVO regulates genes involved in anterior/posterior/germ plasm specification including bcd, exu, swa, osk, nos, aub, pgc, and gcl.
source: These include genes involved in anterior/posterior/germ plasm specification (bcd, exu, swa, osk, nos, aub, pgc, gcl), egg activation (png, plu, gnu, wisp, C(3)g, mtrm), translational regulation (cup, orb, bru1, me31B), and vitelline membrane formation (fs(1)N, fs(1)M3, clos).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data showing OVO binding and expression changes for these genes.

claim: OVO regulates genes involved in egg activation including png, plu, gnu, wisp, C(3)g, and mtrm.
source: These include genes involved in anterior/posterior/germ plasm specification (bcd, exu, swa, osk, nos, aub, pgc, gcl), egg activation (png, plu, gnu, wisp, C(3)g, mtrm), translational regulation (cup, orb, bru1, me31B), and vitelline membrane formation (fs(1)N, fs(1)M3, clos).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data showing OVO binding and expression changes for these genes.

claim: OVO regulates genes involved in translational regulation including cup, orb, bru1, and me31B.
source: These include genes involved in anterior/posterior/germ plasm specification (bcd, exu, swa, osk, nos, aub, pgc, gcl), egg activation (png, plu, gnu, wisp, C(3)g, mtrm), translational regulation (cup, orb, bru1, me31B), and vitelline membrane formation (fs(1)N, fs(1)M3, clos).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data showing OVO binding and expression changes for these genes.

claim: OVO regulates genes involved in vitelline membrane formation including fs(1)N, fs(1)M3, and clos.
source: These include genes involved in anterior/posterior/germ plasm specification (bcd, exu, swa, osk, nos, aub, pgc, gcl), egg activation (png, plu, gnu, wisp, C(3)g, mtrm), translational regulation (cup, orb, bru1, me31B), and vitelline membrane formation (fs(1)N, fs(1)M3, clos).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data showing OVO binding and expression changes for these genes.

claim: OVO is a master transcriptional regulator of oocyte development.
source: This suggests that OVO is a master transcriptional regulator of oocyte development and is responsible for the expression of structural components of the egg as well as maternally provided RNAs that are required for early embryonic development.
evidence: This is inferred from the broad range of essential maternal genes regulated by OVO.

claim: OVO is responsible for the expression of structural components of the egg.
source: This suggests that OVO is a master transcriptional regulator of oocyte development and is responsible for the expression of structural components of the egg as well as maternally provided RNAs that are required for early embryonic development.
evidence: This is supported by data showing OVO regulation of vitelline membrane genes.

claim: OVO is responsible for the expression of maternally provided RNAs that are required for early embryonic development.
source: This suggests that OVO is a master transcriptional regulator of oocyte development and is responsible for the expression of structural components of the egg as well as maternally provided RNAs that are required for early embryonic development.
evidence: This is supported by data showing OVO regulation of genes expressed in 0-2 hour embryos.

claim: Germline stem cells asymmetrically divide to renew the stem cell population and send one daughter cell towards oogenesis.
source: Germline stem cells (GSCs) asymmetrically divide to renew the stem cell population and send one daughter cell towards oogenesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila oogenesis.

claim: In the germarium, oogenesis is preceded by four rounds of incomplete mitotic divisions resulting in a 16-cell egg chamber.
source: In the germarium, oogenesis is preceded by four rounds of incomplete mitotic divisions resulting in a 16-cell egg chamber.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila oogenesis.

claim: One cell is specified as the oocyte, which is arrested in prophase of meiosis I, while the rest of the 15 cells enter endoreplication cycles and become nurse cells.
source: One cell is specified as the oocyte, which is arrested in prophase of meiosis I, while the rest of the 15 cells enter endoreplication cycles and become nurse cells (NCs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila oogenesis.

claim: Once the 16-cell egg chamber buds from the germarium, the nurse cells begin to transcribe and translate a vast array of RNAs and proteins that serve diverse functional roles.
source: Once the 16-cell egg chamber buds from the germarium, the NCs begin to transcribe and translate a vast array of RNAs and proteins that serve diverse functional roles (Bastock and St Johnston, 2008; Spradling et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Maternal RNAs and proteins position in correct spatial orientation to support anterior/posterior and dorsal ventral axis specification.
source: These roles include positioning maternal mRNAs and proteins in the correct spatial orientation to support anterior/posterior, and dorsal ventral axis specification, as well negative regulators of translation to ensure that the maternal mRNAs are not translated before fertilization (Lasko, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Negative regulators of translation ensure that maternal mRNAs are not translated before fertilization.
source: These roles include positioning maternal mRNAs and proteins in the correct spatial orientation to support anterior/posterior, and dorsal ventral axis specification, as well negative regulators of translation to ensure that the maternal mRNAs are not translated before fertilization (Lasko, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The oocyte contains proteins and mRNAs needed for egg activation, completion of meiosis and initiation of embryonic development after fertilization.
source: The oocyte also contains a number of proteins and mRNAs that are needed for egg activation, completion of meiosis and initiation of embryonic development after fertilization (Avilés-Pagán and Orr-Weaver, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Germ cells in the developing embryo need to be specified and maintained separately from somatic cells.
source: To repeat the process of oogenesis from generation to generation, germ cells in the developing embryo need to be specified and maintained separately from the rest of the developing somatic cell population.
evidence: This is established knowledge about germline development.

claim: Germ cell specification requires maternally controlled localization of the germ plasm and early pole cell formation in the embryo.
source: This requires maternally controlled localization of the germ plasm and early pole cell formation in the embryo (Mahowald, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Transcriptional regulation driving the expression of maternal pathways is less well understood than the interactions between maternally supplied mRNAs and proteins.
source: While the complex interactions between maternally supplied mRNAs and proteins have been well studied, transcriptional regulation driving the expression of these pathways are less well understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Few positive regulators of female-specific germ cell transcription have been identified.
source: Few positive regulators of female-specific germ cell transcription have been identified.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: grauzone (grau) activates the transcription of cortex in the female germline.
source: Genes such as grauzone (grau) and maternal gene required for meiosis (mamo) have been shown to activate the transcription of cortex and vasa, respectively, in the female germline (Harms et al., 2000; Nakamura et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: maternal gene required for meiosis (mamo) activates the transcription of vasa in the female germline.
source: Genes such as grauzone (grau) and maternal gene required for meiosis (mamo) have been shown to activate the transcription of cortex and vasa, respectively, in the female germline (Harms et al., 2000; Nakamura et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Active repression of male-specific transcription through the activity of egg, wde, and Su(var)205 is important for female germline cellular identity and oocyte development.
source: Active repression of male-specific transcription through the activity of egg, wde, and Su(var)205 (Smolko et al., 2018), or global repression of non-ovarian transcriptional networks through the function of sov (Benner et al., 2019), have shown the importance of heterochromatin formation in the female germline for cellular identity and oocyte development.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Global repression of non-ovarian transcriptional networks through the function of sov shows the importance of heterochromatin formation in the female germline for cellular identity and oocyte development.
source: Active repression of male-specific transcription through the activity of egg, wde, and Su(var)205 (Smolko et al., 2018), or global repression of non-ovarian transcriptional networks through the function of sov (Benner et al., 2019), have shown the importance of heterochromatin formation in the female germline for cellular identity and oocyte development.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Transcriptional repression, mediated through changes in histone modifications, is a key regulator of egg chamber differentiation.
source: In fact, recent work has shown the importance of transcriptional repression, mediated through changes in histone modifications, as a key regulator of egg chamber differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent work.

claim: GSCs exist in a 'ground state' of histone modifications characterized by modest non-canonical repressive H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 histone marks at many genes, as well as transcriptionally active H3K27ac histone marks and open chromatin at others.
source: GSCs have been shown to exist in a sort of 'ground state' of histone modifications. Characterized with modest non-canonical repressive H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 histone marks at many genes, as well as transcriptionally active H3K27ac histone marks and open chromatin at others (Pang et al., 2023; DeLuca et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: As oocyte development continues, repressive histone marks associated with heterochromatin increase in abundance resulting in fewer histone marks associated with transcription and open chromatin.
source: As oocyte development continues, repressive histone marks associated with heterochromatin begin to increase in abundance resulting in fewer histone marks associated with transcription and open chromatin.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Gene expression becomes more restricted throughout the differentiation process in oogenesis.
source: This suggests that gene expression becomes more restricted throughout the differentiation process.
evidence: This is inferred from the increase in repressive histone marks during oocyte development.

claim: It is unlikely that the female germline directs oocyte development solely through a repressive transcriptional model.
source: However, it is unlikely that the female germline directs oocyte development solely through a repressive transcriptional model.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the need for active transcription during oogenesis.

claim: Female germ cells that are ovo– do not survive into adulthood.
source: Female germ cells that are ovo– do not survive into adulthood (Oliver et al., 1987; Oliver et al., 1990; Benner et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Hypomorphic ovo alleles that disrupt the transcriptional activator OVO-B show an arrested egg chamber phenotype.
source: Hypomorphic ovo alleles, specifically ones that disrupt the transcriptional activator OVO-B, show an arrested egg chamber phenotype, indicating that wild-type OVO-B activity is required for oocyte maturation (Salles et al., 2002; Benner et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Wild-type OVO-B activity is required for oocyte maturation.
source: Hypomorphic ovo alleles, specifically ones that disrupt the transcriptional activator OVO-B, show an arrested egg chamber phenotype, indicating that wild-type OVO-B activity is required for oocyte maturation (Salles et al., 2002; Benner et al., 2023).
evidence: This is inferred from the arrested egg chamber phenotype in hypomorphic alleles.

claim: Germline OVO is expressed at all stages of oogenesis.
source: Germline OVO is expressed at all stages of oogenesis, where it is eventually maternally loaded into the egg.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Maternal OVO becomes specifically localized to the developing germline and persists throughout embryogenesis until zygotic OVO is expressed.
source: Maternal OVO becomes specifically localized to the developing germline and persists throughout embryogenesis until zygotic OVO is expressed (Hayashi et al., 2017; Benner et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: OVO is eternally expressed in the female germline.
source: Thus, OVO is eternally expressed in the female germline, suggesting it may be a key regulator of female-specific germline transcription.
evidence: This is inferred from the continuous expression from oogenesis through embryogenesis.

claim: Only two downstream targets have previously been identified for OVO: ovo itself and ovarian tumor (otu).
source: However, only two downstream targets have previously been identified for OVO.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: OVO positively regulates the expression of its own transcription, executing an autoregulatory loop.
source: OVO has been shown to positively regulate the expression of its own transcription, therefore executing an autoregulatory loop, as well as positively regulating the transcription of the gene ovarian tumor (otu)(Lü et al., 1998; Bielinska et al., 2005; Lü and Oliver, 2001; Andrews et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: otu is required in the female germline.
source: otu is also required in the female germline, where otu– germ cells show viability and germline tumor phenotypes (Bishop and King, 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: otu– germ cells show viability and germline tumor phenotypes.
source: otu is also required in the female germline, where otu– germ cells show viability and germline tumor phenotypes (Bishop and King, 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The ovo phenotype is epistatic to that of otu.
source: The ovo phenotype is epistatic to that of otu, and ectopic otu expression cannot rescue female germ cell death due to loss of ovo (Hinson et al., 1999; Pauli et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Ectopic otu expression cannot rescue female germ cell death due to loss of ovo.
source: The ovo phenotype is epistatic to that of otu, and ectopic otu expression cannot rescue female germ cell death due to loss of ovo (Hinson et al., 1999; Pauli et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ovo must be responsible for activating the transcription of genes in addition to otu for female germ cell survival and differentiation.
source: Therefore, ovo must be responsible for activating the transcription of genes in addition to otu for female germ cell survival and differentiation.
evidence: This is inferred from the epistasis and rescue experiments.

claim: OVO-B is the predominant protein isoform expressed from the ovo locus in the female germline.
source: OVO-B, the predominant protein isoform expressed from the ovo locus in the female germline (Benner et al., 2023), is a positive regulator of transcription (Andrews et al., 2000) at both the otu and ovo locus.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: OVO-B is a positive regulator of transcription at both the otu and ovo locus.
source: OVO-B, the predominant protein isoform expressed from the ovo locus in the female germline (Benner et al., 2023), is a positive regulator of transcription (Andrews et al., 2000) at both the otu and ovo locus.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Transgenic reporter constructs of otu and ovo require OVO-binding sites both at and upstream of the TSS to recapitulate full reporter expression.
source: Transgenic reporter constructs of otu and ovo require OVO-binding sites both at and upstream of the TSS in order to recapitulate full reporter expression (Bielinska et al., 2005; Lü et al., 1998; Lü and Oliver, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Females hemizygous for antimorphic dominant gain-of-function (ovoD) alleles lack germ cells in the adult ovary.
source: Females hemizygous for antimorphic dominant gain-of-function (ovoD) or homozygous recessive (ovoD1rv) ovo alleles lack germ cells in the adult ovary (Oliver et al., 1987; Benner et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Females homozygous recessive for ovoD1rv alleles lack germ cells in the adult ovary.
source: Females hemizygous for antimorphic dominant gain-of-function (ovoD) or homozygous recessive (ovoD1rv) ovo alleles lack germ cells in the adult ovary (Oliver et al., 1987; Benner et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: True OVO-B null alleles created by deletion of the ovo-B promoter have the same germ cell loss phenotype as ovoD and ovoD1rv alleles.
source: True OVO-B null alleles created by deletion of the ovo-B promoter have the same germ cell loss phenotype (Benner et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The ovoD1rv phenotype is epistatic to otu–.
source: The ovoD1rv phenotype is epistatic to otu–, and ectopic otu+ in ovo– germ cells does not rescue the germ cell death phenotype (Hinson et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Ectopic otu+ in ovo– germ cells does not rescue the germ cell death phenotype.
source: The ovoD1rv phenotype is epistatic to otu–, and ectopic otu+ in ovo– germ cells does not rescue the germ cell death phenotype (Hinson et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The OVO-GFP ChIP dataset had 7235 significant ChIP peaks genome-wide.
source: The OVO-GFP ChIP dataset had 7235 significant ChIP peaks according to peak enrichment analysis genome-wide, while OVO-HA ChIP dataset had 3393 significant peaks genome-wide (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on peak calling analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claim: The OVO-HA ChIP dataset had 3393 significant peaks genome-wide.
source: The OVO-GFP ChIP dataset had 7235 significant ChIP peaks according to peak enrichment analysis genome-wide, while OVO-HA ChIP dataset had 3393 significant peaks genome-wide (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on peak calling analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claim: The Jaccard index between OVO-HA and OVO-GFP ChIP peaks was 0.64.
source: The Jaccard index between OVO-HA and OVO-GFP ChIP peaks was 0.64 (where 0=no overlap and 1=full overlap) with a total of 3094 ChIP peaks overlapping.
evidence: This is calculated from the overlap of ChIP-seq peaks.

claim: 3094 ChIP peaks overlap between OVO-HA and OVO-GFP datasets.
source: The Jaccard index between OVO-HA and OVO-GFP ChIP peaks was 0.64 (where 0=no overlap and 1=full overlap) with a total of 3094 ChIP peaks overlapping.
evidence: This is calculated from the overlap of ChIP-seq peaks.

claim: 91% of OVO-HA peaks overlapped OVO-GFP peaks.
source: Thus, almost all significant OVO-HA ChIP peaks were also found within the OVO-GFP ChIP dataset (91% of OVO-HA peaks overlapped OVO-GFP peaks).
evidence: This is calculated from the overlap of ChIP-seq peaks.

claim: The most significant motif found in OVO ChIP peaks is 5'-TAACGGTAAA-3', found in 49% of significant OVO ChIP peaks.
source: The most significant motif, 5'-TAACGGTAAA-3', was found in 49% of significant OVO ChIP peaks (Figure 1D, 'Motif One').
evidence: This is derived from de novo motif enrichment analysis using STREME on ChIP peaks.

claim: The de novo OVO motif is highly similar to previously reported OVO DNA binding motifs 5'-AGTAACNGT-3' and 5'-TGTAACNGT-3'.
source: This motif is highly similar to the OVO DNA binding motif that has been reported twice before, 5'-AGTAACNGT-3' (SELEX method, 'Garfinkel OVO Motif') and 5'-TGTAACNGT-3' (Footprinting method, 'Oliver OVO Motif').
evidence: This is based on comparison of the de novo motif with previously published motifs.

claim: The core OVO-binding sequence is 5'-TAACNGT-3'.
source: Collectively, this is strong evidence that the core OVO-binding sequence is 5'-TAACNGT-3'.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of multiple motif analyses.

claim: The motif 5'-GWGMGAGMGAGABRG-3' was found in 18% of OVO ChIP peaks and is a significant match to the DNA binding motifs of GAF (Trl) and CLAMP.
source: The motif 5'-GWGMGAGMGAGABRG-3' (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) was found in 18% of OVO ChIP peaks and is a significant match to the DNA binding motifs of the transcription factors GAF (Trl) (Omelina et al., 2011) and CLAMP (Soruco et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on motif enrichment analysis and comparison to known motifs.

claim: Trl germline clones are not viable, indicating that GAF activity is required in the germline during oogenesis.
source: Trl germline clones are not viable, indicating that GAF activity is required in the germline during oogenesis (Chen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: 72% of OVO ChIP peaks contain at least one variation of the four OVO binding motifs.
source: Searching for all variations of the OVO DNA binding motif (Supplementary file 3) within our significant overlapping ChIP peaks indicated that 72% of peaks contained at least one variation of these four binding motifs.
evidence: This is based on motif searching in ChIP peaks.

claim: The read density for all ChIP peaks that contain each one of the de novo OVO motifs, as well as the in vitro OVO motifs, are centered over the motif location.
source: We found that the read density for all ChIP peaks that contain each one of the de novo OVO motifs, as well as the in vitro OVO motifs, are centered over the motif location (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is based on analysis of ChIP-seq read density centered on motif locations.

claim: OVO ChIP peaks are spatially enriched near TSS/promoter locations and not correlated with ORF and TTS locations.
source: Measuring the relative distance of our OVO ChIP peaks to TSS, ORFs, and TTS, showed that the OVO binding was highly enriched near TSS/promoter locations and was not correlated with ORF and TTS locations (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is based on analysis of relative distance of ChIP peaks to gene elements.

claim: 45% of OVO ChIP peaks directly overlapped a TSS.
source: Although OVO ChIP peaks overlapping genes showed a strong read density enrichment over the TSS, we found that only 45% (1394/3094) of OVO ChIP peaks directly overlapped a TSS.
evidence: This is based on overlap analysis of ChIP peaks with annotated TSSs.

claim: 43% of OVO ChIP peaks were found to overlap the gene body downstream of the TSS.
source: 43% (1339/3094) of OVO ChIP peaks were found to overlap the gene body downstream of the TSS (intronic and exonic sequences) and 12% (366/3094) did not overlap any gene elements, indicating that they were intergenic.
evidence: This is based on overlap analysis of ChIP peaks with gene elements.

claim: 12% of OVO ChIP peaks did not overlap any gene elements, indicating that they were intergenic.
source: 43% (1339/3094) of OVO ChIP peaks were found to overlap the gene body downstream of the TSS (intronic and exonic sequences) and 12% (366/3094) did not overlap any gene elements, indicating that they were intergenic.
evidence: This is based on overlap analysis of ChIP peaks with gene elements.

claim: CAGEr predicted 6,856 significant TSSs in the ovary dataset.
source: CAGEr predicted 6,856 significant TSSs in the ovary dataset, of which 1047 overlapped with OVO ChIP peaks.
evidence: This is based on CAGE-seq analysis of ovary tissue.

claim: 1047 ovary CAGE-seq TSSs overlapped with OVO ChIP peaks.
source: CAGEr predicted 6,856 significant TSSs in the ovary dataset, of which 1047 overlapped with OVO ChIP peaks.
evidence: This is based on overlap analysis of CAGE-seq TSSs with ChIP peaks.

claim: OVO is binding at or near TSSs of genes actively being transcribed in the ovary.
source: Furthermore, OVO is binding at or near TSSs of genes actively being transcribed in the ovary.
evidence: This is inferred from the overlap of OVO ChIP peaks with CAGE-seq TSSs.

claim: GSC ATAC and H3K27ac read density showed a high degree of enrichment over OVO ChIP peak maximums.
source: GSC ATAC and H3K27ac read density showed a high degree of enrichment over OVO ChIP peak maximums (Figure 2A) and OVO DNA binding motifs (Figure 2B), consistent with positive transcriptional activity.
evidence: This is based on analysis of ATAC-seq and histone ChIP-seq data at OVO binding sites.

claim: GSC H3K4me3 read density was enriched with OVO ChIP peak maximums and OVO DNA binding motifs.
source: GSC H3K4me3 read density was, to a lesser extent, also enriched with OVO ChIP peak maximums and OVO DNA binding motifs.
evidence: This is based on analysis of histone ChIP-seq data at OVO binding sites.

claim: There was no read density enrichment for repressive GSC H3K27me3 and H3K9me3 histone marks at OVO ChIP peak maximums and OVO DNA binding motifs.
source: However, there was no read density enrichment for repressive GSC H3K27me3 and H3K9me3 histone marks.
evidence: This is based on analysis of histone ChIP-seq data at OVO binding sites.

claim: There was an even higher read density enrichment over OVO ChIP peak maximum and DNA binding motifs for 32 c ATAC-seq data compared to GSC.
source: Notably, there was an even higher read density enrichment over OVO ChIP peak maximum and DNA binding motifs for 32 c ATAC-seq data, while read density enrichment decreased for 32 C H3K27ac histone mark (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of ATAC-seq data at OVO binding sites in 32c egg chambers.

claim: Read density enrichment decreased for 32 C H3K27ac histone mark compared to GSC.
source: Notably, there was an even higher read density enrichment over OVO ChIP peak maximum and DNA binding motifs for 32 c ATAC-seq data, while read density enrichment decreased for 32 C H3K27ac histone mark (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of histone ChIP-seq data at OVO binding sites in 32c egg chambers.

claim: There is a significant enrichment in overlapping peaks genome-wide between OVO and GSC ATAC (p<0.001, odds ratio = 75.9).
source: A Fisher's exact test indicated a significant enrichment in overlapping peaks genome-wide between OVO and GSC ATAC (p<0.001, odds ratio = 75.9), 32 c NC ATAC (p<0.001, odds ratio = Infinite), GSC H3K27ac (p<0.001, odds ratio = 31.7), GSC H3K4me3 (p<0.001, odds ratio = 12.0), and 32 c NC H3K27ac (p<0.001, odds ratio = 7.9) peaks.
evidence: This is based on Fisher's exact test of peak overlap.

claim: There is a significant enrichment in overlapping peaks genome-wide between OVO and 32 c NC ATAC (p<0.001, odds ratio = Infinite).
source: A Fisher's exact test indicated a significant enrichment in overlapping peaks genome-wide between OVO and GSC ATAC (p<0.001, odds ratio = 75.9), 32 c NC ATAC (p<0.001, odds ratio = Infinite), GSC H3K27ac (p<0.001, odds ratio = 31.7), GSC H3K4me3 (p<0.001, odds ratio = 12.0), and 32 c NC H3K27ac (p<0.001, odds ratio = 7.9) peaks.
evidence: This is based on Fisher's exact test of peak overlap.

claim: There is a significant enrichment in overlapping peaks genome-wide between OVO and GSC H3K27ac (p<0.001, odds ratio = 31.7).
source: A Fisher's exact test indicated a significant enrichment in overlapping peaks genome-wide between OVO and GSC ATAC (p<0.001, odds ratio = 75.9), 32 c NC ATAC (p<0.001, odds ratio = Infinite), GSC H3K27ac (p<0.001, odds ratio = 31.7), GSC H3K4me3 (p<0.001, odds ratio = 12.0), and 32 c NC H3K27ac (p<0.001, odds ratio = 7.9) peaks.
evidence: This is based on Fisher's exact test of peak overlap.

claim: There is a significant enrichment in overlapping peaks genome-wide between OVO and GSC H3K4me3 (p<0.001, odds ratio = 12.0).

evidence: This is based on Fisher's exact test of peak overlap.

source: A Fisher's exact test indicated a significant enrichment in overlapping peaks genome-wide between OVO and GSC ATAC (p<0.001, odds ratio = 75.9), 32 c NC ATAC (p<0.001, odds ratio = Infinite), GSC H3K27ac (p<0.001, odds ratio = 31.7), GSC H3K4me3 (p<0.001, odds ratio = 12.0), and 32 c NC H3K27ac (p<0.001, odds ratio = 7.9) peaks.

evidence: This is based on Fisher's exact test of peak overlap.

evidence: This is based on Fisher's exact test of peak overlap.

claim: There is a significant depletion in overlapping peaks genome-wide between OVO and 8 c NC H3K9me3 (p<0.001, odds ratio = 0.5).
source: While there was a significant depletion in overlapping peaks genome-wide between OVO and 32 c NC H3K27me3 (p<0.001, odds ratio = 0.6), GSC H3K9me3 (p<0.001, odds ratio = 0.7), and 8 c NC H3K9me3 (p<0.001, odds ratio = 0.5).
evidence: This is based on Fisher's exact test of peak overlap.

claim: OVO-bound promoters have an increase in accessibility when compared to non-OVO bound promoters.
source: However, we did notice an increase in enrichment for OVO-bound promoters compared to OVO non-bound promoters (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G), possibly suggesting that OVO-bound promoters are more open or have an increase in accessibility when compared to non-OVO bound promoters.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of ATAC-seq signal at OVO-bound vs non-bound promoters.

claim: OVO binding genome-wide is tightly associated with open chromatin regardless of germ cell stage.
source: Altogether suggesting that OVO binding genome-wide is tightly associated with open chromatin regardless of germ cell stage, and active transcription in GSCs.
evidence: This is based on analysis of ATAC-seq data at different developmental stages.

claim: OVO binding is associated with active transcription in GSCs.
source: Altogether suggesting that OVO binding genome-wide is tightly associated with open chromatin regardless of germ cell stage, and active transcription in GSCs.
evidence: This is based on analysis of H3K27ac data in GSCs.

claim: OVO DNA binding motifs are evenly distributed around promoters.
source: Like OVO ChIP peaks, OVO DNA binding motifs were highly enriched at or near the TSS (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of motif distribution relative to TSSs.

claim: OVO DNA binding motifs showed a broad distribution upstream and downstream of the TSS.
source: Significantly, the OVO DNA binding motifs showed a broad distribution upstream and downstream of the TSS.
evidence: This is based on analysis of motif distribution in promoters.

claim: There is a significant enrichment for INR in ovary promoters that overlapped an OVO ChIP peak compared to ovary promoters that did not overlap an OVO ChIP peak (p<0.01, odds ratio = 1.70).
source: We found a significant enrichment for INR (p<0.01, odds ratio = 1.70), DPE (p<0.01, odds ratio = 1.81), MTE (p<0.01, odds ratio = 1.65), and most importantly, OVO DNA binding motifs (p<0.01, odds ratio = 4.83), in ovary promoters that overlapped an OVO ChIP peak in comparison to the subset of ovary promoters that did not overlap an OVO ChIP peak (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is based on motif enrichment analysis in CAGE-seq promoters.

claim: There is a significant enrichment for DPE in ovary promoters that overlapped an OVO ChIP peak compared to ovary promoters that did not overlap an OVO ChIP peak (p<0.01, odds ratio = 1.81).
source: We found a significant enrichment for INR (p<0.01, odds ratio = 1.70), DPE (p<0.01, odds ratio = 1.81), MTE (p<0.01, odds ratio = 1.65), and most importantly, OVO DNA binding motifs (p<0.01, odds ratio = 4.83), in ovary promoters that overlapped an OVO ChIP peak in comparison to the subset of ovary promoters that did not overlap an OVO ChIP peak (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is based on motif enrichment analysis in CAGE-seq promoters.

claim: There is a significant enrichment for MTE in ovary promoters that overlapped an OVO ChIP peak compared to ovary promoters that did not overlap an OVO ChIP peak (p<0.01, odds ratio = 1.65).
source: We found a significant enrichment for INR (p<0.01, odds ratio = 1.70), DPE (p<0.01, odds ratio = 1.81), MTE (p<0.01, odds ratio = 1.65), and most importantly, OVO DNA binding motifs (p<0.01, odds ratio = 4.83), in ovary promoters that overlapped an OVO ChIP peak in comparison to the subset of ovary promoters that did not overlap an OVO ChIP peak (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is based on motif enrichment analysis in CAGE-seq promoters.

claim: There is a significant enrichment for OVO DNA binding motifs in ovary promoters that overlapped an OVO ChIP peak compared to ovary promoters that did not overlap an OVO ChIP peak (p<0.01, odds ratio = 4.83).
source: We found a significant enrichment for INR (p<0.01, odds ratio = 1.70), DPE (p<0.01, odds ratio = 1.81), MTE (p<0.01, odds ratio = 1.65), and most importantly, OVO DNA binding motifs (p<0.01, odds ratio = 4.83), in ovary promoters that overlapped an OVO ChIP peak in comparison to the subset of ovary promoters that did not overlap an OVO ChIP peak (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is based on motif enrichment analysis in CAGE-seq promoters.

claim: OVO-bound promoters are more likely to contain INR, DPE, MTE, and OVO DNA binding motifs than non-OVO-bound promoters.
source: This indicates that OVO-bound promoters are more likely to contain these specific promoter elements than non-OVO-bound promoters.
evidence: This is inferred from the enrichment analysis of promoter elements.

claim: Promoters containing INR and DPE, but lacking TATA-box elements, are common among Drosophila gonad promoters compared to promoters of other tissue types.
source: As has been described before, promoters containing INR and DPE, but lacking TATA-box elements, are common among Drosophila gonad promoters compared to promoters of other tissue types (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The presence of TATA-box elements is negatively associated with germline-specific gene expression.
source: The presence of TATA-box elements is negatively associated with germline-specific gene expression (FitzGerald et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: TATA-box elements were significantly depleted in ovary CAGE-seq promoters when compared to testes (p<0.01, odds ratio = 0.78).
source: We found that TATA-box elements were significantly depleted in ovary CAGE-seq promoters when compared to testes (p<0.01, odds ratio = 0.78; Figure 3E) or digestive system (p<0.01, odds ratio = 0.50; Figure 3F) CAGE-seq promoters.
evidence: This is based on motif enrichment analysis comparing different tissues.

claim: TATA-box elements were significantly depleted in ovary CAGE-seq promoters when compared to digestive system (p<0.01, odds ratio = 0.50).
source: We found that TATA-box elements were significantly depleted in ovary CAGE-seq promoters when compared to testes (p<0.01, odds ratio = 0.78; Figure 3E) or digestive system (p<0.01, odds ratio = 0.50; Figure 3F) CAGE-seq promoters.
evidence: This is based on motif enrichment analysis comparing different tissues.

claim: Both ovo and otu have TATA-less promoters.
source: Indeed, both ovo and otu have TATA-less promoters.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the promoter sequences of these genes.

claim: OVO bound promoters are characterized by the presence of INR, DPE, MTE, and OVO DNA binding motifs.
source: Briefly, OVO bound promoters are characterized by the presence of INR, DPE, MTE, and, of course, OVO DNA binding motifs.
evidence: This is a summary of the motif enrichment analysis.

claim: The distribution of OVO DNA binding motifs in ovary promoters is not fixed relative to TSSs or other core promoter elements.
source: Importantly, the distribution of OVO DNA binding motifs in ovary promoters is not fixed relative to TSSs or other core promoter elements.
evidence: This is based on analysis of motif spacing relative to TSSs.

claim: It is highly unlikely that OVO acts as a female germline RNA polymerase complex member that anchors the complex to the core promoter and helps determine the + 1 mRNA nucleotide.
source: Thus, it is highly unlikely that OVO acts as a female germline RNA polymerase complex member that anchors the complex to the core promoter and helps determine the + 1 mRNA nucleotide.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of precise motif spacing.

claim: The imprecise location of OVO-binding sites might suggest that OVO is more likely to facilitate the binding of other basal transcriptional factors.
source: Rather, the imprecise location of OVO-binding sites might suggest that OVO is more likely to facilitate the binding of other basal transcriptional factors.
evidence: This is speculated based on the motif distribution analysis.

claim: ovoovo-GAL4/ovoΔBP transheterozygous allelic combination greatly reduces OVO activity resulting in sterility, however, female germ cells are able to survive up until at least stage 5 of oogenesis.
source: Previous work from our lab has identified a transheterozygous ovo allelic combination (ovoovo-GAL4/ovoΔBP) that greatly reduces OVO activity resulting in sterility, however, female germ cells are able to survive up until at least stage 5 of oogenesis (Benner et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The T2A-GAL4-3xSTOP insertion in ovoovo-GAL4 would disrupt roughly 90% of the ovo-B transcripts.
source: Importantly, this insertion in the extended exon 3 would disrupt roughly 90% of the ovo-B transcripts.
evidence: This is inferred from the location of the insertion relative to splice junctions.

claim: About 10% of ovo-B transcripts utilize an upstream splice junction in exon 3 and would not be disrupted with the T2A-GAL4-3xSTOP insertion.
source: However, since about 10% of ovo-B transcripts utilize an upstream splice junction in exon 3, these transcripts would not be disrupted with the T2A-GAL4-3xSTOP insertion and thus allow for enough OVO activity for germ cell survival (Benner et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Driving expression of UASp-3xFHA-OVO-B rescues the arrested germ cell phenotype of ovoovo-GAL4/ovoΔBP ovaries.
source: Since ovoovo-GAL4 expresses GAL4 in place of full-length OVO due to the T2A sequences, we can drive expression of a rescuing OVO-B construct downstream of UASp to generate OVO+ female germ cells, which in fact does rescue the arrested germ cell phenotype of ovoovo-GAL4/ovoΔBP ovaries.
evidence: This is based on experimental observation of rescue.

claim: 1994 genes primarily expressed in the germline significantly increased in expression with ectopic rescue OVO.
source: The differential expression analysis indicated that 1994 genes primarily expressed in the germline (see next paragraph) significantly increased in expression with ectopic rescue OVO (Figure 4C, cyan/purple dots) and 2924 genes primarily expressed in the soma (see next paragraph) significantly decreased in expression with ectopic rescue OVO expression (Figure 4C, yellow/blue dots).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq differential expression analysis.

claim: 2924 genes primarily expressed in the soma significantly decreased in expression with ectopic rescue OVO expression.
source: The differential expression analysis indicated that 1994 genes primarily expressed in the germline (see next paragraph) significantly increased in expression with ectopic rescue OVO (Figure 4C, cyan/purple dots) and 2924 genes primarily expressed in the soma (see next paragraph) significantly decreased in expression with ectopic rescue OVO expression (Figure 4C, yellow/blue dots).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq differential expression analysis.

claim: 5886 genes were not considered to be differentially expressed in the RNA-seq analysis.
source: A total of 5886 genes were not considered to be differentially expressed in our analysis (Figure 4C, gray dots).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq differential expression analysis.

claim: 2,298 genes that were expressed in the RNA-seq data overlapped an OVO ChIP peak.
source: We found that 2,298 genes that were expressed in our RNA-seq data overlapped an OVO ChIP peak.
evidence: This is based on integration of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: 666 genes significantly increased in expression and were bound by OVO, which is a significant enrichment (p<0.01, odds ratio = 2.21).
source: 666 genes significantly increased in expression and were bound by OVO, which is a significant enrichment according to a Fisher's exact test (Figure 4C, cyan dots, p<0.01, odds ratio = 2.21).
evidence: This is based on Fisher's exact test of overlap between ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: 564 genes decreased in expression and were bound by OVO, indicating a significant depletion (p<0.01, odds ratio = 0.85).
source: While conversely, 564 genes decreased in expression and were bound by OVO, indicating a significant depletion according to a Fisher's exact test (Figure 4C, blue dots, p<0.01, odds ratio = 0.85).
evidence: This is based on Fisher's exact test of overlap between ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: Genes that are bound by OVO transcriptionally respond in a positive manner.
source: This strongly suggests that genes that are bound by OVO, transcriptionally respond in a positive manner.
evidence: This is inferred from the enrichment of upregulated genes among OVO-bound genes.

claim: 71% of genes (1409/1994) that had a significant increase in expression in the presence of ectopic rescue OVO were found to be expressed in 0–2 hr old embryos.
source: We found that 71% of genes (1409/1994) that had a significant increase in expression in the presence of ectopic rescue OVO were found to be expressed in 0–2 hr old embryos (Figure 4D, green dots), while only 21% of genes (625/2,924) that had a significant decrease in expression were found in the same embryo dataset (Figure 4D, yellow dots).
evidence: This is based on cross-referencing RNA-seq data with modENCODE embryo data.

claim: Only 21% of genes (625/2,924) that had a significant decrease in expression were found in 0-2 hr old embryos.
source: We found that 71% of genes (1409/1994) that had a significant increase in expression in the presence of ectopic rescue OVO were found to be expressed in 0–2 hr old embryos (Figure 4D, green dots), while only 21% of genes (625/2,924) that had a significant decrease in expression were found in the same embryo dataset (Figure 4D, yellow dots).
evidence: This is based on cross-referencing RNA-seq data with modENCODE embryo data.

claim: There is a significant enrichment for genes that significantly increased in expression and were present in 0–2 hr old embryos (p<0.01, odds ratio = 2.8).
source: A Fisher's exact test confirmed that there was a significant enrichment for genes that significantly increased in expression and were present in 0–2 hr old embryos (p<0.01, odds ratio = 2.8).
evidence: This is based on Fisher's exact test.

claim: There is a significant depletion for genes that significantly decreased in expression and were present in 0–2 hr old embryos (p<0.01, odds ratio = 0.17).
source: In comparison, there was a significant depletion for genes that significantly decreased in expression and were present in 0–2 hr old embryos (p<0.01, odds ratio = 0.17).
evidence: This is based on Fisher's exact test.

claim: Genes that significantly increased in expression were more likely to be expressed in the germline.
source: This result indicated that genes that significantly increased in expression were more likely to be expressed in the germline and that the presence of ectopic rescue OVO significantly increased the expression of genes that were maternally deposited in the early embryo.
evidence: This is inferred from the enrichment in 0-2 hr embryo genes.

claim: The presence of ectopic rescue OVO significantly increased the expression of genes that were maternally deposited in the early embryo.
source: This result indicated that genes that significantly increased in expression were more likely to be expressed in the germline and that the presence of ectopic rescue OVO significantly increased the expression of genes that were maternally deposited in the early embryo.
evidence: This is inferred from the enrichment in 0-2 hr embryo genes.

claim: The set of genes that significantly decrease in expression are not enriched in the embryo and are more likely specific to somatic cell gene expression.
source: While the set of genes that significantly decrease in expression are not enriched in the embryo and are more likely specific to somatic cell gene expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the depletion in 0-2 hr embryo genes.

claim: OVO appears to be a positively acting transcription factor in the germline.
source: In terms of the germline proper, OVO appears to be a positively acting transcription factor.
evidence: This is inferred from the overall pattern of gene expression changes.

claim: A significant OVO ChIP peak was found overlapping the TSS of ovo-B, with four significant OVO DNA binding motifs present.
source: A significant OVO ChIP peak was found overlapping the TSS of ovo-B, with four significant OVO DNA binding motifs present (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq and motif analysis at the ovo locus.

claim: ATAC-seq, H3K27ac, and H3K4me3 peaks overlapped the ovo promoter.
source: ATAC-seq, H3K27ac, and H3K4me3 peaks overlapped the ovo promoter.
evidence: This is based on integration of ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq data at the ovo locus.

claim: otu had a positive transcriptional response to the presence of OVO rescue (log2 fold change = 2.41; p-adj <0.001).
source: It was also evident that otu had a positive transcriptional response to the presence of OVO rescue (log2 fold change = 2.41; p-adj <0.001).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq differential expression analysis at the otu locus.

claim: OVO binds and positively regulates both itself and otu in vivo.
source: These results confirm that OVO binds and positively regulates both itself and otu in vivo, as previous work has indicated.
evidence: This is confirmed by ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: 525 genes contained an OVO ChIP peak overlapping the transcriptional start site and significantly increased in expression in the presence of rescue OVO.
source: To be especially stringent, we focused on the genes that contained an OVO ChIP peak overlapping the transcriptional start site and significantly increased in expression in the presence of rescue OVO. A total of 525 genes met these criteria.
evidence: This is based on integration of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: Biological process GO term enrichment analysis on 525 genes showed a significant enrichment for 45 GO terms.
source: Biological process GO term enrichment analysis on these 525 genes showed a significant enrichment for 45 GO terms (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is based on GO term enrichment analysis.

claim: The significant GO terms were almost exclusively related to female reproduction and maternal control of early embryonic development.
source: The significant GO terms were almost exclusively related to female reproduction and maternal control of early embryonic development (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on GO term enrichment analysis.

claim: OVO expression in adult gonads is essential for constructing an egg and depositing maternal RNAs to support zygotic embryonic development.
source: These GO terms are well understood in the context of oogenesis and broadly suggest that OVO expression in adult gonads is essential for constructing an egg and depositing maternal RNAs to support zygotic embryonic development.
evidence: This is inferred from the GO term enrichment analysis.

claim: bicoid, exuperantia, and swallow are essential for anterior specification of the embryo.
source: For example, bicoid (Figure 6B), and bicoid mRNA binding proteins exuperantia (exu) and swallow (swa), are essential for anterior specification of the embryo (Lasko, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: bicoid, exuperantia, and swallow were occupied by OVO in vivo, significantly upregulated by OVO-B, and had OVO motifs in close proximity to the TSS.
source: All these genes were occupied by OVO in vivo, significantly upregulated by OVO-B, and had OVO motifs in close proximity to the TSS.
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq, RNA-seq, and motif analysis.

claim: oskar and nanos are involved in posterior patterning.
source: Genes involved in posterior patterning (oskar and nanos; Figure 6C), as well as pole cell specification genes (polar granule component, germ cell-less, and aubergine; Lasko, 2012; Benner et al., 2018), also showed similar RNA-seq, ChIP-seq, and OVO DNA binding motif profiles as ovo and otu.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: polar granule component, germ cell-less, and aubergine are pole cell specification genes.
source: Genes involved in posterior patterning (oskar and nanos; Figure 6C), as well as pole cell specification genes (polar granule component, germ cell-less, and aubergine; Lasko, 2012; Benner et al., 2018), also showed similar RNA-seq, ChIP-seq, and OVO DNA binding motif profiles as ovo and otu.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: cup, maternal expression at 31B, oo18 RNA-binding protein, and bruno 1 are involved in translational silencing and regulation of maternally provided mRNAs.
source: Genes that are involved in translational silencing and regulation of maternally provided mRNAs, such as cup (Figure 6D), maternal expression at 31B (me31B), oo18 RNA-binding protein (orb), and bruno 1 (bru1), as well as essential genes involved in meiosis completion and egg activation after fertilization (giant nuclei (gnu), pan gu (png), plutonium (plu), wispy (wisp), C(3)G, and matrimony (mtrm)) (Figure 6E; Lasko, 2012; Avilés-Pagán and Orr-Weaver, 2018) all show this stereotypic pattern of promoter proximal OVO occupancy and DNA binding motifs, and OVO-dependent transcription.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: giant nuclei, pan gu, plutonium, wispy, C(3)G, and matrimony are essential genes involved in meiosis completion and egg activation after fertilization.
source: Genes that are involved in translational silencing and regulation of maternally provided mRNAs, such as cup (Figure 6D), maternal expression at 31B (me31B), oo18 RNA-binding protein (orb), and bruno 1 (bru1), as well as essential genes involved in meiosis completion and egg activation after fertilization (giant nuclei (gnu), pan gu (png), plutonium (plu), wispy (wisp), C(3)G, and matrimony (mtrm)) (Figure 6E; Lasko, 2012; Avilés-Pagán and Orr-Weaver, 2018) all show this stereotypic pattern of promoter proximal OVO occupancy and DNA binding motifs, and OVO-dependent transcription.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: OVO is a central transcription factor activating the expression of essential maternal and early embryonic development pathways in the female germline.
source: These data indicate that the OVO is a central transcription factor activating the expression of essential maternal and early embryonic development pathways in the female germline.
evidence: This is inferred from the broad range of essential genes regulated by OVO.

claim: fs(1)N, fs(1)M3, and closca were all bound by OVO and responded transcriptionally to the presence of ectopic rescue OVO.
source: We also found that the genes fs(1)N, fs(1)M3, and closca, were all bound by OVO and responded transcriptionally to the presence of ectopic rescue OVO.
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: fs(1)N, fs(1)M3, and closca are expressed in the germline and the encoded proteins are eventually incorporated into the vitelline membrane providing the structural integrity and impermeability of the egg.
source: These genes are significant because they constitute a set of genes that are expressed in the germline and the encoded proteins are eventually incorporated into the vitelline membrane providing the structural integrity and impermeability of the egg (Mineo et al., 2017; Ventura et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Loss-of-function of fs(1)N, fs(1)M3, and closca results in flaccid eggs that are permeable to dye and fail to develop.
source: Loss-of-function of these three genes results in flaccid eggs that are permeable to dye and fail to develop.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The loss-of-function phenotype of fs(1)N, fs(1)M3, and closca closely resembles the dominant antimorph ovoD3 phenotype.
source: The loss-of-function phenotype of fs(1)N, fs(1)M3, and closca closely resembles the dominant antimorph ovoD3 phenotype.
evidence: This is based on comparison of phenotypes.

claim: ovoD3/ovo+ transheterozygous females express a repressive form of OVO that results in dominant sterility.
source: ovoD3/ovo+ transheterozygous females express a repressive form of OVO that results in dominant sterility, and importantly, these females lay flaccid eggs with compromised vitelline membranes that are permeable to the dye neutral red (Oliver et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: ovoD3/ovo+ females lay flaccid eggs with compromised vitelline membranes that are permeable to the dye neutral red.
source: ovoD3/ovo+ transheterozygous females express a repressive form of OVO that results in dominant sterility, and importantly, these females lay flaccid eggs with compromised vitelline membranes that are permeable to the dye neutral red (Oliver et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: It is plausible that the repressive OVOD3 is negatively regulating fs(1)N, fs(1)M3, and closca that are required for vitelline membrane formation.
source: Since OVO+ is bound at the TSS of fs(1)N, fs(1)M3, and closca, and these three genes respond transcriptionally to OVO+, then it is plausible that the repressive OVOD3 is negatively regulating these three genes that are required for vitelline membrane formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of phenotypes and OVO binding.

claim: OVO is essential for regulating genes that are required for egg integrity and maturation.
source: This is evidence that OVO is not only involved in regulating the expression of numerous essential maternal pathways for embryonic development, but it is also essential for regulating genes that are required for egg integrity and maturation.
evidence: This is inferred from the regulation of vitelline membrane genes.

claim: OVO binds and positively regulates a large array of genes required to build an egg and pattern the resulting embryo after fertilization.
source: Our work here significantly expands our knowledge on OVO function in the female germline, showing that OVO binds and positively regulates a large array of genes required to build an egg and pattern the resulting embryo after fertilization.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: OVO accomplishes regulation by directly binding to the promoters of its targets, as well as more distant sites that could represent enhancers.
source: OVO accomplishes this by directly binding to the promoters of its targets, as well as more distant sites that could represent enhancers.
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data showing binding at TSSs and intergenic regions.

claim: Hints of OVO's functions can be found in the hypomorphic and antimorphic ovo alleles which show egg chamber arrest, ventralized eggs, and permeable vitelline membranes.
source: Hints of these functions can be found in the hypomorphic and antimorphic ovo alleles which show egg chamber arrest, ventralized eggs, and permeable vitelline membranes.
evidence: This is based on prior knowledge of ovo phenotypes.

claim: OVO is required to activate multiple pathways involved in oocyte and early embryonic development.
source: It is clear that OVO is required to activate multiple pathways involved in oocyte and early embryonic development.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings.

claim: OVO bound to the promoters and increased the expression of bcd, exu, and swa, all involved in ensuring correct anterior specification of the embryo.
source: For example, OVO bound to the promoters and increased the expression of bcd, and the bcd mRNA binding proteins exu and swa, all involved in ensuring correct anterior specification of the embryo (Lasko, 2012).
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: OVO downstream target genes gnu, png, plu, and wisp all belong in the same interconnected pathway ensuring egg activation.
source: OVO downstream target genes gnu, png, plu, and wisp all belong in the same interconnected pathway ensuring egg activation (Avilés-Pagán and Orr-Weaver, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: OVO controls a battery of genes involved in the positive regulation of RNA binding proteins that negatively regulate translation, including cup, Me31b, bru1, and orb.
source: A similar story was found for genes such as cup, Me31b, bru1, and orb, indicating that OVO controls a battery of genes involved in the positive regulation of RNA binding proteins that negatively regulate translation (Lasko, 2012).
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: OVO bound and positively regulated a number of posterior and germ plasm specification genes such as osk, nos, aub, gcl, and pgc.
source: OVO also bound and positively regulated a number of posterior and germ plasm specification genes such as osk, nos, aub, gcl, and pgc (Lasko, 2012; Mahowald, 2001).
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: Other important germ plasm factors such as staufen and tudor were not bound by or transcriptionally responsive to OVO.
source: For example, other important germ plasm factors such as staufen and tudor were not bound by or transcriptionally responsive to OVO.
evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: Other transcription factors are responsible for regulating staufen and tudor.
source: This observation suggest that other transcription factors are responsible for regulating these genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of OVO regulation of these genes.

claim: It is unlikely that OVO is a core component of the RNA polymerase complex in the female germline.
source: It is therefore unlikely that OVO is a core component of the RNA polymerase complex in the female germline.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of precise motif spacing.

claim: It is unlikely that OVO is analogous to male specific TATA-associated factors that activate gene expression in the male germline.
source: This suggests that it is unlikely to be analogous to male specific TATA-associated factors that have been shown to activate gene expression in the male germline (Hiller et al., 2004; Hiller et al., 2001; Lu et al., 2020; Li et al., 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of precise motif spacing and comparison to male germline factors.

claim: OVO is an activator of transcription.
source: It is therefore possible, and previously well supported, that OVO is an activator of transcription (Lü et al., 1998; Lü and Oliver, 2001; Bielinska et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by prior work and the current data.

claim: OVO might ensure that the chromatin status of maternally expressed genes remains open.
source: OVO might ensure that the chromatin status of maternally expressed genes remains open.
evidence: This is speculated based on the association of OVO binding with open chromatin.

claim: In GSCs, OVO ChIP peaks largely overlap open chromatin and transcriptionally active histone marks.
source: In GSCs, OVO ChIP peaks largely overlap open chromatin and transcriptionally active histone marks.
evidence: This is based on integration of ChIP-seq with ATAC-seq and histone ChIP-seq data.

claim: In stage 5 egg chambers, there is an even higher degree of association between OVO binding and open chromatin, while the significant association with H3K27ac marks is greatly reduced.
source: However, in stage 5 egg chambers, there was an even higher degree of association with open chromatin (almost all OVO ChIP peaks overlapped ATAC-seq peaks), while the significant association with H3K27ac marks was greatly reduced.
evidence: This is based on integration of ChIP-seq with ATAC-seq and histone ChIP-seq data at different stages.

claim: OVO binding helps to maintain chromatin accessibility, even when the locus in question is no longer actively transcribed.
source: This increase in association with open chromatin and OVO binding, even as the amount of open chromatin is reduced throughout egg chamber differentiation, might indicate that OVO binding helps to maintain chromatin accessibility, even when the locus in question is no longer actively transcribed.
evidence: This is speculated based on the stage-specific chromatin data.

claim: OVO might be more similar in function to pioneer factors/chromatin remodelers than it is to a transcription factor that is only involved in activating transcription.
source: Therefore, OVO might be more similar in function to pioneer factors/chromatin remodelers than it is to a transcription factor that is only involved in activating transcription.
evidence: This is speculated based on the chromatin accessibility data.

claim: Removal of OVO DNA binding sites overlapping the TSS results in a strong decrease in reporter expression.
source: Although we did not test the requirement for OVO DNA binding motifs at other OVO-bound genes in this work, this has been extensively explored before, showing that removal of OVO DNA binding sites overlapping the TSS results in a strong decrease in reporter expression (Lü et al., 1998; Bielinska et al., 2005; Lü and Oliver, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Removal of more distal upstream OVO DNA binding sites also reduces reporter expression to a lesser degree.
source: Removal of more distal upstream OVO DNA binding sites also reduces reporter expression to a lesser degree.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Removal of OVO DNA binding sites while leaving the rest of the enhancer regions intact never totally abolished reporter expression.
source: However, for most cases tested, removal of OVO DNA binding sites while leaving the rest of the enhancer regions intact, never totally abolished reporter expression.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Adding zld DNA binding motifs to a stochastically expressed transcriptional reporter increases the activity and response of the reporter.
source: Adding zld DNA binding motifs to a stochastically expressed transcriptional reporter increases the activity and response of the reporter (Dufourt et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Distally located zld DNA binding motifs influenced reporter expression to a lesser degree than proximal sites.
source: Distally located zld DNA binding motifs influenced reporter expression to a lesser degree than proximal sites.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: A single zld DNA binding site adjacent to the TSS produced the strongest reporter activity.
source: A single zld DNA binding site adjacent to the TSS produced the strongest reporter activity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: There is not an absolute requirement for zld DNA binding to activate reporter expression; however, the addition of TSS adjacent zld DNA binding motifs does strongly influence reporter response.
source: Importantly, just like the activity of OVO transgenic reporters, there is not an absolute requirement for zld DNA binding to activate reporter expression; however, the addition of TSS adjacent zld DNA binding motifs does strongly influence reporter response.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and comparison to OVO.

claim: zld achieves reporter response through its pioneering activity.
source: We know that zld achieves this reporter response through its pioneering activity (Xu et al., 2014; Harrison et al., 2011), whether OVO achieves this similar effect on gene expression through a shared mechanism, or in cooperation with other transcription factors needs to be further explored.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.
